title: Median slew: annotated latency vs cost brief
content:
Purpose:
This is a working brief to capture a compact benchmark comparing median-latency behavior (and cost implications) across three serving configurations when exposed to rapid changes in arrival rate ("slew"). The goal is to produce simple, actionable guidance for routing policies and warmup sizing for pods.

Background / motivation:
- Most SLO conversations focus on p95/p99 tail; median shifts matter for cost-sensitive interactive workloads because median moves drive per-token amortization and batching efficiency.
- We observed customers pay large incremental cost during short surges even when tails are bounded because median increases (lower batch density, cold slot overhead).

Experiment summary (short):
- Target model: 13B transformer (float16 baseline), request distribution: 50–200 tokens per request, mean=80, sd=40, 2k concurrent sessions simulated.
- Slew profile: linear ramp from 100 rps -> 1,200 rps over 30s (fast slew) and a slower ramp 100 -> 1,200 rps over 5 min (slow slew). Each run repeated 5 times.
- Configurations compared: A) Opportunistic-batch (default continuous-batching, no prewarm), B) Prewarmed-slot (2 reserved prewarm slots per pod), C) Aggressive-quant+prefill (4-bit quantized model variant + prefill KV cache reuse).
- Metric focus: median latency (ms), p95 latency (ms), cost-per-1M-tokens ($), and batch fill-factor (avg tokens per batch).

Input assumptions and environment:
- Hardware: A100 80GB equivalent.
- Pricing: baseline inference cost calibrated to $0.60 / 1000 tokens (hosted list unit for comparison) — we report relative delta instead of hard billing lines.
- Sim harness: synthetic sessionized traffic generator with sticky sessions, realistic session interleaving (idle time distribution Weibull k=1.3).

Results (aggregated numbers, median of 5 runs):

ASCII table: aggregated (fast slew / slow slew rows)

Config | slew | median (ms) | p95 (ms) | batch fill | rel cost
-------+------+------------+----------+------------+--------
A Opportunistic | fast | 138	| 430	| 6.2 tokens	| 1.00x
A Opportunistic | slow | 94	| 350	| 9.8 tokens	| 0.93x
B Prewarm-2 | fast | 86	| 280	| 10.5 tokens	| 1.18x
B Prewarm-2 | slow | 78	| 265	| 11.1 tokens	| 1.12x
C Agg-quant+prefill | fast | 110	| 370	| 8.9 tokens	| 0.78x
C Agg-quant+prefill | slow | 76	| 260	| 12.0 tokens	| 0.70x

Key observations:
- Median sensitivity to slew rate: Opportunistic batching (A) shows the largest median delta between fast and slow slew (+47 ms). That reduction is explained by lower batch fill during fast slew due to startup friction and fewer session coalescences.
- Prewarm reduces median and p95 during fast slew but increases relative cost (reserve overhead). For short-lived spikes (<60s), prewarm's cost amortization is marginal unless the spike is repeated frequently.
- Quantization + prefill (C) offers the best cost reduction while keeping close to prewarm latencies on slow slew; however, on very fast slew median still trails prewarm by ~24 ms — this is primarily kernel cold path and KV cache miss recovery.
- Batch fill correlates strongly with median (Spearman rho 0.78 across runs). Improving fill is the single biggest lever for median reductions.

Micro-annotations: why medians move during slew
- Slot cold-activation: when new slots boot for surge, initial tokens pay cold overhead (resource init + kernel switches) that elevates median across the pool because surge arrivals are spread across many newly activated slots.
- Session stickiness breakdown: when many sessions ramp quickly, continuous-batcher cannot match session affinity, reducing cross-session packing.
- Prefill helps because KV cache priming keeps per-session kernel hot and increases effective token throughput per slot.

Visual (text) sparkline: median vs time (fast slew, config rows). timeline buckets 6s
- A: ▅▃▂▁▁▁▁▁▂▃▅▇ (ramp shows big jump then slow settle)
- B: ▂▂▂▁▁▁▁▁▂▂▂ (much flatter)
- C: ▂▂▂▁▁▁▁▁▂▂▃ (close to B, small bump)

Tradeoffs and heuristics (operational takeaways):
- If bursts are frequent (duty cycle > 20%) and predictable: prefer prewarm sizing set to expected peak sessions / shard. Rough sizing formula: prewarm_slots_per_pod = ceil(peak_sessions_per_pod / 8).
- If bursts are infrequent but cost-sensitive: use quant+prefill variant and adaptive routing where heavy requests route to quant-variants during high load (fallback to float16 for quality-critical calls).
- For mixed workloads (chat + long-form generation): prioritize prefill on chat endpoints (short tokens, many sessions) and opportunistic batching on long-form paths.
- Short ramp detection (<=30s): consider a temporary aggressive prewarm policy with time-decay (auto-scale down after 60s of tailing low load) to amortize warm cost over the spike window.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quality-vs-quant tradeoff: need a small A/B eval on 4-bit quant variant for our top-10 prompt set to quantify generation delta and decide fallback rules.
- Longer-term: integrate a predictive slew model in router that uses recent session velocity to pre-create slots (probabilistic prewarm).
- Cost modeling: translate rel-cost into actual billing for billing tiers (hosted vs dedicated) and evaluate under customer-specific price curves.

Immediate next steps (owners):
- Run 50-run stress to tighten confidence intervals for config C on the fast slew (Evan) — due 2026-04-08.
- Small prompt-level A/B for quant quality on customer-critical prompts (Priya) — due 2026-04-12.
- Prototype a decay-based prewarm policy (Liam) and add a knob in Console to preview cost delta.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Might try hybrid policy: keep 1 warm slot per pod + probabilistic prefill cycles triggered by arrival second-derivative threshold.
- Consider adding a small per-slot warm cache of recent KV to reduce miss penalty during churn.

Attachments / artifacts used:
- Traffic harness config: jira JIRA-RELAY-789
- Raw traces (s3 refs in linked artifacts) and PR with harness changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/642

Status: draft — want feedback from SRE and serving runtime on whether prefill kernel changes are feasible without regressing throughput.

-- end of brief (working)
